title: Sthenelus warns; Diomedes refuses retreat
intro: The Trojan pair advances, but Diomedes refuses to mount his own chariot and withdraw. His reply joins an assertion of inherited courage to confidence in Athena. He is already planning to capture the enemy horses.

notes.text: ἐκφερέμεν is epic infinitive of ἐκφέρω, ‘carry out,’ dependent on the horses’ willingness in the preceding line. ποθέοντε is nominative dual present participle, ‘missing’ Aeneas’ familiar voice. αὐτώ is accusative dual emphatic ‘our very selves,’ with νῶϊ. κτείνῃ and ἐλάσσῃ are subjunctives under the preceding fear μή: Diomedes may kill both men and drive off the horses.

μώνυχας is accusative plural of μῶνυξ, ‘single-hoofed,’ a conventional horse epithet. τέ᾽ is elided τεά, ‘your,’ agreeing with ἅρματα; τεώ agrees with dual ἵππω. δεδέξομαι is a reduplicated future of δέχομαι, ‘I shall receive / face,’ reinforced by instrumental δουρί. Pandarus finally chooses the spear.

The first two participles are plural, while ἐμμεμαῶτε is dual; epic readily alternates the two when describing a pair. βάντες is root-aorist participle of βαίνω. ἔχον, an unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω, here means ‘directed / drove,’ with the horses as object and ἐπί plus dative marking the opponent.

κεχαρισμένε is perfect middle/passive participle of χαρίζομαι in the vocative, ‘dear / pleasing to my heart.’ ἄνδρε and κρατερώ are accusative dual after ὁρόω, the epic uncontracted form of ὁράω. μεμαῶτε is also dual, but ἔχοντας is plural. ἶν᾽ is elided ἶνα, accusative of ἴς, ‘strength,’ modified by ἀπέλεθρον, ‘immeasurable.’

εἰδώς is perfect participle of οἶδα, ‘skilled,’ taking genitive τόξων. εὔχεται means ‘declares / claims,’ not prayer. ἐκγεγάμεν is epic perfect active infinitive of ἐκγίγνομαι, ‘be descended from,’ with genitive Ἀγχίσαο. Aeneas’ divine mother makes him an especially formidable opponent in Sthenelus’ assessment.

χαζώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive, ‘let us withdraw,’ with ἐφ᾽ ἵππων, ‘on the chariot.’ θῦνε is present imperative of θύνω, ‘rush,’ negated by μηδέ. μή πως introduces the feared result; ὀλέσσῃς is epic aorist active subjunctive of ὄλλυμι, ‘lose / destroy.’ φίλον ἦτορ means his own life or heart.

ὑπόδρα means ‘from under lowered brows,’ the conventional hostile look. φόβον δ᾽ represents directional φόβονδε, ‘toward flight,’ rather than φόβον followed by ordinary δέ. πεισέμεν is epic future active infinitive of πείθω, ‘persuade,’ with accusative σέ as subject after οἴω: ‘I do not think even you will persuade me.’

γενναῖον means in keeping with one’s birth or nature. The construction is impersonal, ‘it is not in my nature to fight while shrinking away.’ ἀλυσκάζοντι agrees with μοι in the dative. καταπτώσσειν means ‘cower’; ἔμπεδον, ‘firm, steadfast,’ describes the spirit that remains in him.

ὀκνείω is an epic form of ὀκνέω, ‘shrink from / be reluctant.’ ἐπιβαινέμεν is present infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω. αὔτως means ‘just as I am,’ here without mounting. εἶμι, ‘I shall go,’ is the present with future force; τρεῖν is infinitive of τρέω, ‘flee in fear,’ after ἐᾷ, ‘allows.’

τούτω is accusative dual, ‘these two,’ strengthened by ἄμφω. ἀποίσετον is third-dual future of ἀποφέρω; the horses will not carry both men away. ἡμείων is epic genitive plural ‘us’ after ἀπό. φύγῃσιν is aorist subjunctive of φεύγω with extended -σι: ‘even if one should escape.’

βάλλεο is uncontracted middle imperative of βάλλω, ‘put [this] in your mind.’ ἀμφοτέρω is accusative dual after κτεῖναι, ‘kill both.’ ἐρυκακέειν is an epic infinitive of ἐρυκάκω, ‘hold back,’ used as a command to Sthenelus. αὐτοῦ means ‘right there.’ ἄντυξ is the chariot rail; τείνας, aorist participle of τείνω, describes securing the reins to it.
